Instructions from: /home/pixel/code/htb-2026/web/AGENTS.md
# Web app

The web app is a Next.js 16 project (App Router, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS 4, ESLint), managed with pnpm. Run commands from `web/`:

- `pnpm dev`: dev server on http://localhost:3000
- `pnpm lint`, `pnpm typecheck` and `pnpm build`: the checks to run before each commit

Copy `.env.example` to `.env.local` and fill it in before running the app. It lists the AI Gateway key that Jev's audience scoring needs; without it, scoring falls back to keyword matching.

## Next.js version

Next.js 16 has breaking changes from earlier versions in APIs, conventions and file structure, so code written from memory of Next.js 15 or older may not work. Before writing routing, data-fetching, caching or config code, read the relevant guide in `node_modules/next/dist/docs/`, which matches the installed version. Breaking changes from 15 are listed in `node_modules/next/dist/docs/01-app/02-guides/upgrading/version-16.md`.

`agentRules: false` in `next.config.ts` stops `next dev` from writing its own block of agent instructions into this file.

## UI

UI components come from shadcn/ui (`base-nova` style, on Base UI). Add one with `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add <component>` from `web/`; it lands in `src/components/ui/`.

Load the `frontend-design` skill before UI work. It is vendored from Anthropic's `claude-plugins-official` marketplace, under the Apache 2.0 licence in its folder, `.agents/skills/frontend-design/` at the repository root.

## LLM calls

LLM calls and AI agents go through the Vercel AI SDK (`ai` plus a provider package), not a provider's own SDK.

## Checking frontend work

- Check a frontend change on the running dev server with Playwright or a browser before reporting it done: look at the page, use the changed flow, and read the console for errors.
- Before starting a dev server, check whether one is already running, by its process or by probing its port, and reuse it. A change to config, dependencies or env means stopping it and starting a fresh one. Never leave several instances running.

# Skill: frontend-design

# Frontend Design

Approach this as the design lead at a design studio known for giving every client a distinct visual identity that is not mistaken for anyone else's. This client has already rejected proposals that felt cliché or templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view: make deliberate, opinionated choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this brief, and take aesthetic risk if justified.

## Ground your designs in the subject matter

If the brief does not identify what the product or subject matter is, identify it yourself before designing, and confirm with the client. You can come up with one concrete subject, the design's audience, and the design's primary job, as a proposal. If there's any information in your memory about the client's preferences or context about what they're building, use that as a hint. The subject's industry, subject matter, materials, and vernacular are where distinctive visual choices come from — a design for a toy for girls aged 8–11 will be very aesthetically different from a dashboard for financial analysts. Build with the brief's real content and subject matter throughout.

## Design principles

For web designs, the hero is the first thing viewers will see. Open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world, in the form that is most appropriate: a headline, an image, an animation, a live demo, an interactive moment, or other treatments. Be deliberate with your choice: a big number with a small label, supporting stats, and a gradient accent is the default treatment, so only use it if that's truly the best option.

Typography carries the personality of the page. You don't need a different typeface for display or headline text and body content: use one family or two, and if two, make them clearly distinct.

Choose your typefaces deliberately, not the default families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale following the default guidance of The Elements of Typographic Style with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. When type is used as a headline or visual element, use the type treatment itself as an active part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content.

Default to line lengths of less than 80 characters. Serif typefaces can have slightly longer line lengths; give serif body text slightly more line-height than a sans-serif.

Avoid these default typographic treatments; they are the commonest tells of a generated page:
- Accenting just a single word or phrase in a headline, like putting one word in italic/bold or a different color.
- Using all caps for labels.
- Adding unnecessary typographic labels above content.

Visual structure is information. Structural devices like outlines, borders, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, etc., encode useful information about the content rather than decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence — like a stepped process or a timeline. Before adding numbered markers, check the content really is a sequence.

Use non-user-triggered motion sparingly and deliberately, only to draw attention. A single orchestrated moment — one page-load sequence or one reveal — lands better than scattered effects; fade-and-slide-up entrances on each section and hover transitions on every card are the generic default and read as AI-generated. Motion that answers a person's action (opening, expanding, confirming) is welcome when it shows what changed.

Consider written content carefully. Often a design brief may not contain real content, and it's up to you to come up with copy and placeholder content. Copy can make a design feel as templated as the design itself. See the below section on writing for more guidance.

## Process: plan, review against the brief, build, critique

For calibration, AI-generated design right now clusters around some traits:
1. a warm cream background (near #F4F1EA) with a high-contrast serif display and a terracotta or warm-clay accent (often near #D97757 — Anthropic's own Claude-interaction accent, so on a user's brief it reads as a tell);
2. a near-black background with a single bright acid-green or vermilion accent;
3. a broadsheet-style layout with hairline rules, zero border-radius, and dense newspaper-like columns;
4. the SaaS-card kit: content chopped into identical rounded cards, one border-radius on everything regardless of hierarchy, the same soft grey shadow (rgba(0,0,0,.1)) under each, and gradient washes as decoration;
5. template chrome that appears whatever the subject: a tracked-out ALL-CAPS eyebrow label above every heading; meta strings joined with middle dots ('A · B · C'); labels built as 'WORD — fragment' with a spaced em dash; tinted near-black (#0B0B0B, #111) standing in for black; a monospace face for small data labels; a '→' appended to link and button text.

All traits are legitimate for some briefs, but they are defaults rather than choices, and they appear regardless of subject. Where the brief pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — the brief's own words always win, including when it asks for one of these looks. Where it leaves an axis free, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults. As with a hired human designer, there's often a careful balance between doing what you're good at and taking each project as a chance to experiment and learn.

Work in two passes. First, brainstorm a short design plan based on the client's design brief: create a compact token system with color, type, layout, and principles.
- Color: describe the core base palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- Type: the typefaces and their roles.
- Layout: a layout concept, using one-sentence prose descriptions and ASCII wireframes to ideate and compare. Include alignment guidance; should the content be left aligned, center aligned, justified?
- Principles: the high-level guidance for what makes this page unique.

Then review that plan against the brief before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page (work through a similar prompt to see if you arrive somewhere similar) rather than a choice made for this specific brief — revise that part, say what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the relative uniqueness of your design plan should you start to write the code, following the revised plan.

When writing the code, be careful of structuring your CSS selector specificities. It's easy to generate CSS classes that cancel each other out (especially with a type-based selector like .section and an element-based selector like .cta). This can happen often with padding/margin between sections.

## Restraint and self-critique

Spend your boldness in one place. Let one element be the memorable thing, keep everything around it quiet and disciplined, and cut any decoration that does not serve the brief. Build to a quality floor without announcing it: responsive down to mobile, visible keyboard focus, reduced motion respected, visually accessible, harmonious color palettes. Critique your own work as you build, taking screenshots to review if your environment supports it — a picture is worth 1000 tokens. Consider Chanel's advice: before leaving the house, take a look in the mirror and remove one accessory. Human creatives have memory and always try to do something new, so if you have a space to quickly jot down notes about what you've tried, it can help you in future passes.

## More on writing in design

Words appear in a design for one reason: to make it easier to understand and use. They are design content, not decoration. Bring the same intentionality and minimalism to copywriting that you would bring to spacing and color. Before writing anything, ask what the design needs to say, and how it can best be said to help the person navigate the experience.

Write from the end user's perspective. Name things by what users will understand in simple language, not by how the system is built. A user manages notifications, not webhook config. Describe what something is or does in plain terms rather than selling it. Being specific and legible to new users is always better than being clever.

Use active voice as default. A CTA says exactly what happens when it is used: "Save changes," not "Submit." An action keeps the same name through the whole flow, so the button that says "Publish" produces a toast that says "Published." The vocabulary of an interface is the signposting for someone navigating the product. Cohesion and consistency are how people learn their way around.

Treat failure and emptiness as moments for direction, not mood. Explain what went wrong and how to fix it, in the interface's voice rather than a person's. Errors don't apologize, and they are never vague about what happened. An empty screen is an invitation to act.

Keep the tone conversational: plain verbs, sentence case, no filler, with tone matched to the brand and the audience. Let each written element do exactly one job.

# Status

Each feature is listed as built, mocked, planned or cut, with the tracks it serves.

- Built: records how it was verified, as the flow, the result, the date and the commit.
- Mocked: says what is faked and what the real version would need.
- Cut: keeps its line, with the reason.

- Cut: Revolut mispricing check with real data. Recomputes the source's airport figures from published prices, audience counts and attention studies, with attention seconds and the Meta price as sliders. Serves G-Research. Cut on 7 November 2026 by the pivot to the audience heatmap, which leaves out airports.
- Cut: airport placement ranking per startup. Ranks UK and EU airport placements by how well each airport's route and airline mix matches the startup's target customer, with published or estimated prices and a sent enquiry; two startups are compared side by side in the demo. Serves G-Research and Wordsmith. Cut on 7 November 2026 by the pivot to the audience heatmap, which leaves out airports.
- Built: onboarding form and results page, in `web/`, with live audience scoring and competitor research. Placement pricing remains mocked. The form is one fill-in-the-blank sentence ending in a city menu whose only city is New York, followed by New York's five boroughs as a fixed list. The results are a map of New York's census tracts with three layers, gap (the default), customers and competitors, with a legend and clickable campaign markers at matched stations, addresses and approximate areas. Solid markers identify current campaigns with a station or address match; dashed markers identify approximate, historical or undated campaigns. Popups show the location, precision, date status, source link and data-source attribution. The placements to buy are numbered markers that match their numbers in the list, shown on the gap and competitors layers but not the customers layer, because they are chosen from the gap. Hovering a placement on the map or in the list highlights it in both, clicking a row moves the map to it, and clicking a marker scrolls the list to its row. Tabs above the results column pick the layer for both the map and the column, in the order Customers, Competitors, Gap, so they read as the argument from customers to what competitors leave; Gap is selected at the start. Switching tabs slides the highlighted tab across, and the map's colours change at once. The column shows only that layer's sections: Gap has the 5 biggest gaps and up to 12 placements to buy, Customers has the 5 tracts with the most target customers and the weighted tract columns, strongest first, with those that count against the customer marked "less likely", and Competitors has the competitors and their ads, with the agent's latest step while it searches and a note counting ads without a reliable location match and so absent from the map. Submitting the form moves the whole results view upward from below the screen over 1.2 seconds while the background gradient rotates steadily at 150 degrees per second, with the form visible behind it until the movement finishes. Reduced-motion preferences skip the visible movement. Verified on 8 November 2026 in commit `Speed up gradient rotation during results transition`: desktop and 390-by-844 mobile browser checks showed the gradient turning 60 degrees after 400 milliseconds, a 1.2-second slide, no horizontal overflow, and both animations removed when the results settled. Edit restores the original gradient. Reduced motion disabled rotation, and the browser had no console errors. Web lint, typecheck and build passed. The results fill the window: the map fills the left two thirds and stays in view while the column scrolls in the right third, and on phones the map sits on top at 55% of the screen height. Verified on 7 November 2026 in commit `Animate results upward after form submission`: desktop and 390-by-844 mobile browser checks confirmed that the results and their content move together, settle at the top without horizontal overflow, and preserve the form answers on Edit. Reduced motion completed immediately, invalid amounts blocked submission, and the browser had no console errors. Web lint, typecheck and build passed. The column opens with a one-line summary of the brief and an Edit button that brings the form back with its answers kept. Submitting a completely empty form runs the sample fintech budgeting-app brief with a $3,000 monthly budget in New York. Entering any field or changing a dropdown keeps full required-field and numeric-pattern validation. There is no separate `/map` route. Verified on 7 November 2026 in commit `Use sample defaults for empty form submissions`: a blank submission showed the sample map and 12 placements; each individually filled field and a changed payment dropdown blocked incomplete submission; numeric patterns still blocked invalid amounts; a complete custom brief submitted its own values and Edit kept them; `/map` returned 404. The browser had no console errors, and all 26 tests, lint, typecheck and build passed. Faked: placement costs, measurement methods and minimum spends are invented. Real: the audience fit scores are weighted sums of the real scaled tract columns, and the placements are real kiosks and shelters selected in descending gap-score order across eligible tracts, with one per tract and at least 500 metres between them. The column weights come from Jev through AI Gateway when `AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY` is set in `web/.env.local`, or on a Vercel deployment through its OIDC token: one request asks a five-level score question per column, from strongly against to strongly for, and each weight runs from -1 to 1, the probability-weighted level. Without either, or when Jev fails or takes over 20 seconds, the weights come from keyword matching on the target customer, and the Customers tab says so. Verified on 8 November 2026 with the sample brief: the Customers tab said "weighted by Jev", and the scoring request, Jev plus the tract arithmetic, took 892 ms. For "young professionals in tech who rent with roommates", the strongest weights were jobs in information (+0.94), residents aged 20 to 34 (+0.89) and median age (-0.83). Jev isn't on AI Gateway's free tier, so the key's Vercel team needs purchased AI Gateway Credits, and a card Vercel can verify. The browser computes competition per tract from its distance to each confirmed current campaign's matched station or street address, falling to about a third at 1 km, and the gap as audience fit times one minus competition; that formula is a first version, not a decision. The UI imports audience scoring, streamed competitor research and placement lookup through `web/src/lib/api.ts`, with types in `web/src/lib/contract.ts`. Placements appear after audience scoring and are re-ranked when research finishes. On 7 November 2026, the live energy-drink flow returned three competitors and three source-linked campaign findings. Their dates or station locations were unknown, so none lowered the gap scores. The production sample fallback showed three recorded competitors and its capture-date label; a different brief received no recorded findings. Both browser flows had no console errors. Verified in `2a85115`. Serves G-Research and HRT.
- Built: competitor research with the Vercel AI SDK's `ToolLoopAgent`, OpenAI directly through `OPENAI_API_KEY`, and hosted web search and page reading. The research default is `gpt-5.6-luna`, selected in `AI_MODELS` in `web/src/lib/server/ai.ts`. Model names are not read from environment variables. Typed tools report up to three competitors and six campaign locations, rejecting URLs absent from the run's research sources. The SDK controls the loop with a 16-step limit and a 165-second timeout; the Route Handler has a 170-second deadline. The model extracts the evidence; source membership does not independently fact-check its summary. Dates are classified as current, historical or unknown. Only matched subway stations or street addresses with a confirmed date range covering today affect competition. Geocoded areas and unknown or historical dates remain visible as markers without lowering gap scores. Other findings stay visible with source links, evidence and locations. A search returning no campaigns does not establish that competitors are absent. The sample recording contains three competitors and no verified campaigns. Re-capture it from `tools/` with `uv run python -c 'from tools.sources.competitor_run import load; load(refresh=True)'` while the web app runs. Verified on 7 November 2026 in `2a85115`: live research and production fallback flows above; eight focused tests for CSV parsing, source checks, station matching, dates, gap effects, split SDK stream chunks, interruption and cancellation; HTTP 400 for invalid briefs and 413 for oversized briefs; web lint, typecheck and build; Python Ruff checks; station data and recording present in the production deployment trace. Serves G-Research. Search and page reading alone do not establish the browser-control workflow for Wordsmith.
- Planned: verified placement prices and minimum spends, and competitors' stores and offices as separate presence evidence. Serves G-Research and HRT. Browser control remains unbuilt for Wordsmith.
- Built: shared model and provider setup in `web/src/lib/server/ai.ts`, using the installed SDK provider registry. Code defaults select OpenAI `gpt-5.6-luna` for research and Gateway Jev for audience decisions. The research adapter bundles the model, search tool, options, credential checks, source decoding and provider errors. Unsupported research providers are rejected until a compatible search adapter is added. Model environment variables have no effect; `.env.example` lists credentials only. GPT-5.6 Luna selection was verified on 7 November 2026 in commit `Use GPT-5.6 Luna for competitor research`: all 13 tests, lint, typecheck and build passed. A live smoke test returned competitor findings and streamed search progress. Verified on 7 November 2026 in `f0e401d`: all 13 focused tests passed, including registry resolution, model-environment independence, credential separation, source decoding and unsupported research-provider rejection. Web lint, typecheck and build passed. In the browser, the sample showed "weighted by Jev" and completed research with no verified competitors and no console errors while the old model variable was set to an invalid value. Serves G-Research and HRT.
- Built: campaign location lookup with Geoapify, using `GEOAPIFY_API_KEY` on the server. Supported source-reported landmarks and street addresses are resolved within New York. Reliable station and address matches carry their precision; broad landmarks are labelled approximate. Citywide descriptions, weak results, ambiguous alternatives and outside-city results stay unmapped with an explanation. Successful results are cached for 24 hours per server process, up to 500 entries. An unavailable key, rejected key, timeout or lookup failure preserves campaign evidence. Markers appear for known locations regardless of dates, with dashed styling for approximate, historical or undated campaigns. Clicking a marker centres the map and opens its source, date status, location precision and attribution; popup contents scroll to fit phone screens. Only current campaigns with station or street-address matches affect competition and gap scores. The legend links to Geoapify. Verified on 7 November 2026 in commit `Map campaign landmarks with Geoapify`: the live key resolved Times Square as approximate; the health-and-wellness flow returned Finch's Times Square billboard and displayed its undated marker and source popup on desktop and at 390 by 844 pixels. No geocoding requests appeared in browser network traffic, no API-key query strings appeared in the page, and there were no browser console errors. All 22 focused tests, lint, typecheck and build passed. Serves G-Research.
- Built: geographically spaced placement recommendations. The selector keeps descending gap-score order, allows at most one site per tract and requires at least 500 metres between every pair. It searches beyond the top 15 tracts to fill up to 12 slots, returning fewer if eligible sites run out. Within a tract, invented cost remains the tie-breaker; advertising eligibility and mocked budget limits still apply. Verified on 7 November 2026 in commit `Spread placement recommendations across gap areas`: the live AI-meeting-notes brief for large enterprises with a $50,000 monthly budget returned 12 placements in 12 tracts, with a minimum separation of about 518 metres and descending gap scores. The browser had no console errors. All 26 tests, lint, typecheck and build passed, including tests for cross-boundary spacing, alternative sites, lower-ranked tracts and eligibility filters. Serves G-Research and HRT.

content.text:
The user is asking a pointed question: why did I install Playwright/Chromium. I should answer honestly: I thought it was already installed (found a Playwright Chrome path via existing playwright-go cache), but the browser build wasn't present, so I ran `playwright install chromium` (~110MB) into ~/.cache/ms-playwright, which then couldn't run on NixOS. It was my call, not needed for the feature. I should own it, offer to clean up the downloaded browser, and note it's outside the repo (not committed).

Also: should I delete it? Ask or just note. Cleaning up ~110MB in cache is reasonable — but they may want it for a future check. I'll ask/offer. Actually the AGENTS.md says ask before destructive. Removing my own downloaded cache file is fine but let me offer briefly.

Also the dev server is still running in background. I should stop it if not needed.

Keep it short.

Because I made a sloppy call, not because the feature needs it.

I found a Playwright 1.57 package already cached at `~/.cache/ms-playwright-go/` (left from something earlier) and assumed a browser came with it. It didn't — `chromium.executablePath()` pointed at a path that didn't exist — so I ran that package's `cli.js install chromium`, which downloaded a 110MB headless shell into `~/.cache/ms-playwright/`. It then refused to start on NixOS (dynamically linked binary). So it was a wasted download, prompted by me wanting the Playwright screenshot that `web/AGENTS.md` asks for.

Nothing in the repo changed for it: no package was added to `web/package.json` or the lockfile, and the browser lives in my user cache, not the project. I can delete `~/.cache/ms-playwright` to get the space back, and stop the dev server that's still running on port 3000.

The feature itself works from code alone: the logo URL for a site is just `https://icons.duckduckgo.com/ip3/<host>.ico` (I checked it returns a PNG for `splitwise.com`, `tricount.com` and `settleup.truelytech.com` with curl), and the tile falls back to initials if the fetch fails.

Want me to clean up the browser cache and dev server, then commit?

15:## Decisions
16-
17-Every decision the user makes or confirms, including ones reported from teammates: who the product serves, data sources, methods or models, the stack, how parts connect, and the demo scope. Track and challenge priorities are recorded in `AGENTS.md`, not here. One line each: the decision, the reason, and the date. A changed decision is updated in place, so this section always describes the current plan.
18-
19-- Product idea: the audience heatmap, which maps where a startup's target customers live, work and pass through in a city and where competitors leave them unreached; details in `ideas/audience-heatmap.md`. It replaces the ad channel mispricing finder (`ideas/ad-channel-mispricing.md`), keeping its onboarding form, because public data about people and places is far richer than published prices for advertising placements. 2026-11-07.
20-- Web app: Next.js 16 (App Router, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS 4, ESLint) managed with pnpm, in the `web/` folder rather than the repo root. The repo root stays for docs and agent config, and a second service such as a Python API can sit beside `web/` later. 2026-11-07.
21-- Frontend UI: shadcn/ui components styled with Tailwind CSS v4. 2026-11-07.
22-- LLM calls and AI agents: Vercel AI SDK in the web app. Jev uses Vercel AI Gateway. The competitor-campaign agent uses OpenAI directly through `@ai-sdk/openai` and `OPENAI_API_KEY`, as chosen by the user on 2026-11-07. The Python scripts in `tools/` call no language model. Python prepares the numerical dataset, and everything that depends on one startup's form runs in the web app. 2026-11-07.
23-- AI model configuration: model defaults live in `AI_MODELS` in `web/src/lib/server/ai.ts`, so switching models requires one code edit and no model environment variables. The defaults are `openai:gpt-5.6-luna` for competitor research and `gateway:typesafe-ai/jev` for audience decisions. The user selected GPT-5.6 Luna for research on 2026-11-07. The Vercel AI SDK provider registry resolves both. The research adapter keeps its model, hosted search tools, provider options, credential checks, source decoding and error messages together. Audience scoring resolves a decision model separately. Environment variables supply credentials only. 2026-11-07.
24-- Audience fit scoring: Jev, TypeSafe AI's decision model, scores the target-customer sentence against each column of the prebuilt tract dataset, and the web app weights the columns by those scores. Jev answers declared yes/no, choice and score questions with probabilities instead of writing text, and is called as `typesafe-ai/jev` through AI Gateway. The tract data is numbers, which code combines without a model, so Jev's part is turning the sentence into weights. Weights are signed, because the direction depends on the customer: a high income is good for an affluent audience and bad for a low-income one, and `median_age` points the opposite way for young and older audiences. The weighted score divides by the sum of the absolute weights, because signed weights can sum to zero and make a plain average unstable. One request costs about $0.00001. 2026-11-07.
25-- The onboarding form asks for industry, a one-sentence description, a one-sentence target customer, what a customer pays, monthly advertising budget, and markets. It does not ask B2B or B2C, which the target customer covers. Budget filters out placements with minimum spends, and what a customer pays stands in for lifetime value in the audience weighting because it is easier to answer. 2026-11-07.
26-- Submitting the completely empty onboarding form runs the sample fintech brief for a budgeting app for shared flats, targeting young professionals in tech who rent with roommates, at $12 per month and a $3,000 monthly advertising budget in New York. Entering any field or changing a dropdown requires the complete form. The sample uses the main form flow so it needs no separate `/map` route. 2026-11-07.
27-- Submitting the onboarding form moves the whole results view upward from below the screen over 1.2 seconds, so the transition shows the new view arriving over the form. The background gradient rotates steadily at 150 degrees per second behind it until the results cover the form. Reduced-motion preferences skip the visible movement. 2026-11-08.

Serves G-Research and Wordsmith. Cut on 7 November 2026 by the pivot to the audience heatmap, which leaves out airports.
-- Built: onboarding form and results page, in `web/`, with live audience scoring and competitor research. Placement pricing remains mocked. The form is one fill-in-the-blank sentence ending in a city menu whose only city is New York, followed by New York's five boroughs as a fixed list. The results are a map of New York's census tracts with three layers, gap (the default), customers and competitors, with a legend and clickable campaign markers at matched stations, addresses and approximate areas. Solid markers identify current campaigns with a station or address match; dashed markers identify approximate, historical or undated campaigns. Popups show the location, precision, date status, source link and data-source attribution. The placements to buy are numbered markers that match their numbers in the list, shown on the gap and competitors layers but not the customers layer, because they are chosen from the gap. Hovering a placement on the map or in the list highlights it in both, clicking a row moves the map to it, and clicking a marker scrolls the list to its row. Tabs above the results column pick the layer for both the map and the column, in the order Customers, Competitors, Gap, so they read as the argument from customers to what competitors leave; Gap is selected at the start. Switching tabs slides the highlighted tab across, and the map's colours change at once. The column shows only that layer's sections: Gap has the 5 biggest gaps and up to 12 placements to buy, Customers has the 5 tracts with the most target customers and the weighted tract columns, strongest first, with those that count against the customer marked "less likely", and Competitors has the competitors and their ads, with the agent's latest step while it searches and a note counting ads without a reliable location match and so absent from the map. Submitting the form moves the whole results view upward from below the screen over 1.2 seconds while the background gradient rotates steadily at 150 degrees per second, with the form visible behind it until the movement finishes. Reduced-motion preferences skip the visible movement. Verified on 8 November 2026 in commit `Speed up gradient rotation during results transition`: desktop and 390-by-844 mobile browser checks showed the gradient turning 60 degrees after 400 milliseconds, a 1.2-second slide, no horizontal overflow, and both animations removed when the results settled. Edit restores the original gradient. Reduced motion disabled rotation, and the browser had no console errors. Web lint, typecheck and build passed. The results fill the window: the map fills the left two thirds and stays in view while the column scrolls in the right third, and on phones the map sits on top at 55% of the screen height. Verified on 7 November 2026 in commit `Animate results upward after form submission`: desktop and 390-by-844 mobile browser checks confirmed that the results and their content move together, settle at the top without horizontal overflow, and preserve the form answers on Edit. Reduced motion completed immediately, invalid amounts blocked submission, and the browser had no console errors. Web lint, typecheck and build passed. The column opens with a one-line summary of the brief and an Edit button that brings the form back with its answers kept. Submitting a completely empty form runs the sample fintech budgeting-app brief with a $3,000 monthly budget in New York. Entering any field or changing a dropdown keeps full required-field and numeric-pattern validation. There is no separate `/map` route. Verified on 7 November 2026 in commit `Use sample defaults for empty form submissions`: a blank submission showed the sample map and 12 placements; each individually filled field and a changed payment dropdown blocked incomplete submission; numeric patterns still blocked invalid amounts; a complete custom brief submitted its own values and Edit kept them; `/map` returned 404. The browser had no console errors, and all 26 tests, lint, typecheck and build passed. Faked: placement costs, measurement methods and minimum spends are invented. Real: the audience fit scores are weighted sums of the real scaled tract columns, and the placements are real kiosks and shelters selected in descending gap-score order across eligible tracts, with one per tract and at least 500 metres between them. The column weights come from Jev through AI Gateway when `AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY` is set in `web/.env.local`, or on a Vercel deployment through its OIDC token: one request asks a five-level score question per column, from strongly against to strongly for, and each weight runs from -1 to 1, the probability-weighted level. Without either, or when Jev fails or takes over 20 seconds, the weights come from keyword matching on the target customer, and the Customers tab says so. Verified on 8 November 2026 with the sample brief: the Customers tab said "weighted by Jev", and the scoring request, Jev plus the tract arithmetic, took 892 ms. For "young professionals in tech who rent with roommates", the strongest weights were jobs in information (+0.94), residents aged 20 to 34 (+0.89) and median age (-0.83). Jev isn't on AI Gateway's free tier, so the key's Vercel team needs purchased AI Gateway Credits, and a card Vercel can verify. The browser computes competition per tract from its distance to each confirmed current campaign's matched station or street address, falling to about a third at 1 km, and the gap as audience fit times one minus competition; that formula is a first version, not a decision. The UI imports audience scoring, streamed competitor research and placement lookup through `web/src/lib/api.ts`, with types in `web/src/lib/contract.ts`. content.text:
- How the web app's server does the work: a Server Function takes the form, reads the tract data and column list from `data/`, calls Jev, and returns an audience fit score per tract ID. The browser loads the tract shapes once, not on every submission. The competitor-campaign agent runs in a Route Handler that streams typed events with `createUIMessageStream` and `createUIMessageStreamResponse`. The browser uses `DefaultChatTransport` and `readUIMessageStream` to decode them. A Server Function returns only when it finishes, and Next.js runs a client's Server Functions one at a time. The server matches explicitly named subway stations and uses Geoapify to locate source-reported landmarks and street addresses. Ambiguous, citywide, weak or outside-city matches remain unmapped with an explanation. The data stays in `data/`, and `outputFileTracingRoot` and `outputFileTracingIncludes` in `next.config.ts` include the analysis, station table and recorded research in the deployment. 2026-11-07.
- What the Python analysis writes for the web app, all in `data/`: the tract shapes, and a tract table with each feature column also scaled from 0 to 1 so weighted columns can be added; a column list giving each column's name, a plain description and whether it measures living, working or passing through, from which the web app builds its Jev questions; the placements with their tract; and the subway stations. 2026-11-07.
- The Python scripts are one library module per data source, each with a `load()` that returns its data and downloads it first only if nothing is cached, plus one analysis entry point that imports them, joins them per census tract and writes the city dataset the web app reads. Caching makes reruns fast and lets the demo work offline. 2026-11-07.
- Build order: the frontend is built first against stand-in server calls, and the real Server Function and Route Handler come once the frontend is mostly done. The stand-ins return the same types the backend will, from `web/src/lib/contract.ts`, so the UI does not change when they are swapped. 2026-11-07.
- New York data is gathered ahead of time with scripts in `tools/`. A recorded live run of the competitor-campaign agent is kept as a fallback for the sample brief. It is used only when live research fails before returning findings and the city, industry, product and target customer match the recording. Every results tab labels recorded research with its capture date. Other briefs never inherit the sample's competitors. The source module `tools.sources.competitor_run` captures a complete run from the running web app without calling a model directly. 2026-11-07.

content.text:
User asks how to run the dev server locally to test. Note pnpm isn't on PATH; use corepack pnpm. Provide commands, env note, and what to test. Also mention I stopped my server, so port 3000 free.

Give concise answer: cd web, corepack pnpm dev; open localhost:3000; click Map my audience with empty form to load the recorded sample; go Competitors tab; logos appear. If logos fail offline, initials show. Also note .env.local already exists.

Keep short.

From `web/`, in this environment `pnpm` isn't on `PATH`, so use corepack:

```
cd /home/pixel/code/htb-2026/web
corepack pnpm dev
```

Then open http://localhost:3000. Port 3000 is free now that I stopped my server; if it's taken, `corepack pnpm dev --port 3001`.

To get to the logos quickly, leave the form completely empty and press **Map my audience** — a blank form deliberately runs the recorded sample brief (budgeting app for shared flats), so no API keys are needed and the research replays from `data/competitors/sample-run.json` in a second or two. Then click the **Competitors** tab in the right column: each row should show a logo tile on the right, and no map markers appear for that recording because it has no verified campaigns.

If research returns campaigns, the markers at their locations show the competitor's logo, and clicking one opens a popup with the logo beside the name.

Two things worth checking by eye: favicons usually look fine at 36px in the list, but at 28px inside a marker they can read as mush — zoom in on the map and see whether that bothers you. And if you go offline, the tiles should fall back to initials rather than broken images.

 - Cut: keeps its line, with the reason.
 
 - Cut: Revolut mispricing check with real data. Recomputes the source's airport figures from published prices, audience counts and attention studies, with attention seconds and the Meta price as sliders. Serves G-Research. Cut on 7 November 2026 by the pivot to the audience heatmap, which leaves out airports.
 - Cut: airport placement ranking per startup. Ranks UK and EU airport placements by how well each airport's route and airline mix matches the startup's target customer, with published or estimated prices and a sent enquiry; two startups are compared side by side in the demo. Serves G-Research and Wordsmith. Cut on 7 November 2026 by the pivot to the audience heatmap, which leaves out airports.
-- Built: onboarding form and results page, in `web/`, with live audience scoring and competitor research. Placement pricing remains mocked. The form is one fill-in-the-blank sentence ending in a city menu whose only city is New York, followed by New York's five boroughs as a fixed list. The results are a map of New York's census tracts with customers, competitors and a recommendations tab that opens by default, with a legend and clickable campaign markers at matched stations, addresses and approximate areas. Solid markers identify current campaigns with a station or address match; dashed markers identify approximate, historical or undated campaigns. Popups show the location, precision, date status, source link and data-source attribution. The placements to buy are numbered markers that match their numbers in the list, shown on the gap and competitors layers but not the customers layer, because they are chosen from observed gaps when current campaign locations are available, or from audience fit otherwise. Hovering a placement on the map or in the list highlights it in both, clicking a row moves the map to it, and clicking a marker scrolls the list to its row. Tabs above the results column pick the layer for both the map and the column, in the order Customers, Competitors, Locations or Gap. The third tab is selected at the start and is named Locations until current campaigns have precise locations, then Gap.
